analysis.one_liner: Requires bottled water to meet the same contamination limits as public tap water.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 103rd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA, within 180 days of the EPA setting a contamination limit for public drinking water, to set the same or stricter limit for bottled water. If the FDA failed to act, the EPA's tap water limit would automatically become the bottled water standard. Bottled water currently is regulated separately and, for some contaminants, less strictly than tap water.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy bottled water, often at a large premium over tap water, would get the assurance that what they drink meets the same contamination limits the government sets for public water systems. The bill also allows the FDA to set stricter limits for bottled water where needed, and it removes the FDA's ability to simply delay by making the EPA standard apply automatically if no rule is issued in time.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FDA to set a bottled water quality level for each contaminant at least as stringent as the EPA's maximum contaminant level for public drinking water, and allows a stricter level if needed to protect health [S2][S3].

Includes a default rule: if the Secretary of Health and Human Services does not issue the regulation within 180 days, the EPA's tap water limit automatically becomes the bottled water standard, so inaction cannot block the protection [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Bottled water companies would bear the cost of monitoring and of meeting the same contamination limits as public water systems, and any added compliance costs could be passed on in bottle prices.

drawbacks.text: Matching tap water standards could raise compliance costs for bottled water producers, and those costs would likely be passed on to consumers in the price of bottled water [S3].

The bill allows the FDA to skip a standard if it finds a contaminant occurs in public water systems but not in bottled water sources, which could leave some bottled-water-specific contaminants unaddressed [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is modest but real: bottled water costs consumers far more per gallon than tap water, yet in some cases is held to weaker contamination limits. The costs fall on producers, and any price increase would be small relative to the existing premium bottled water already commands. The main design weakness is the source-based exemption, which could leave gaps for contaminants found in bottled water but not tap water.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it stayed until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative John Bryant of Texas introduced the bill on June 27, 1994, near the end of the two-year session [S1][S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and on July 12, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bottled water producers are better off, since they avoided being held to the same contamination limits as public tap water systems.

for.name: Rep. John W. Bryant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired during the 103rd Congress by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; it sat at the committee and subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so the record shows no pattern of party support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would require bottled water to meet the same contamination limits as public tap water, adding monitoring and compliance costs for producers. Bottled water sells at a large premium partly on an image of purity, so holding it to tap water standards removes a regulatory advantage the industry currently enjoys over the cheaper alternative.
